claim: The readiness potential (RP) is known to precede subjects' reports of their decision to move.
source: The readiness potential (RP)—a key ERP correlate of upcoming action—is known to precede subjects' reports of their decision to move.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Some view the RP preceding conscious decision reports as evidence against a causal role for consciousness in human decision-making and thus against free-will.
source: Some view this as evidence against a causal role for consciousness in human decision-making and thus against free-will.
evidence: This reflects a position held by some researchers in the field, as indicated by the manuscript's framing.

claim: Previous work on the RP focused on arbitrary decisions that are purposeless, unreasoned, and without consequences.
source: But previous work focused on arbitrary decisions—purposeless, unreasoned, and without consequences.
evidence: This characterization of previous work is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: It remains unknown to what degree the RP generalizes to deliberate, more ecological decisions.
source: It remains unknown to what degree the RP generalizes to deliberate, more ecological decisions.
evidence: This is the research gap identified by the authors.

claim: The expected RPs were found for arbitrary decisions in this study.
source: While we found the expected RPs for arbitrary decisions, they were strikingly absent for deliberate ones.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: RPs were strikingly absent for deliberate decisions.
source: While we found the expected RPs for arbitrary decisions, they were strikingly absent for deliberate ones.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: The results and drift-diffusion model are congruent with the RP representing accumulation of noisy, random fluctuations that drive arbitrary but not deliberate decisions.
source: Our results and drift-diffusion model are congruent with the RP representing accumulation of noisy, random fluctuations that drive arbitrary—but not deliberate—decisions.
evidence: This interpretation is based on the experimental data and computational modeling presented in the study.

claim: The results point to different neural mechanisms underlying deliberate and arbitrary decisions.
source: They further point to different neural mechanisms underlying deliberate and arbitrary decisions, challenging the generalizability of studies that argue for no causal role for consciousness in decision-making to real-life decisions.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential RP patterns observed between decision types.

claim: The findings challenge the generalizability of studies that argue for no causal role for consciousness in decision-making to real-life decisions.
source: They further point to different neural mechanisms underlying deliberate and arbitrary decisions, challenging the generalizability of studies that argue for no causal role for consciousness in decision-making to real-life decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: A series of human studies using EEG found neural correlates of decision processes hundreds of milliseconds prior to the moment that subjects reported having consciously decided.
source: Yet a series of human studies using electroencephalography (EEG) (Haggard and Eimer, 1999; Libet et al., 1983; Salvaris and Haggard, 2014), fMRI (Bode and Haynes, 2009; Bode et al., 2011; Soon et al., 2008; Soon et al., 2013), intracranial (Perez et al., 2015), and single-cell recordings (Fried et al., 2011) challenged the veridicality of this common experience. These studies found neural correlates of decision processes hundreds of milliseconds and even seconds prior to the moment that subjects reported having consciously decided.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Studies using fMRI found neural correlates of decision processes seconds prior to the moment that subjects reported having consciously decided.
source: Yet a series of human studies using electroencephalography (EEG) (Haggard and Eimer, 1999; Libet et al., 1983; Salvaris and Haggard, 2014), fMRI (Bode and Haynes, 2009; Bode et al., 2011; Soon et al., 2008; Soon et al., 2013), intracranial (Perez et al., 2015), and single-cell recordings (Fried et al., 2011) challenged the veridicality of this common experience. These studies found neural correlates of decision processes hundreds of milliseconds and even seconds prior to the moment that subjects reported having consciously decided.
evidence: This is supported by citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Libet and colleagues showed that the readiness potential began before subjects reported a conscious decision to act.
source: There, the authors showed that the readiness potential (RP)—a ramp-up in EEG negativity before movement onset, thought to originate from the presupplementary motor area (pre-SMA)—began before subjects reported a conscious decision to act.
evidence: This is a description of Libet's seminal finding.

claim: The RP is thought to originate from the presupplementary motor area (pre-SMA).
source: There, the authors showed that the readiness potential (RP)—a ramp-up in EEG negativity before movement onset, thought to originate from the presupplementary motor area (pre-SMA)—began before subjects reported a conscious decision to act.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the RP's neural origin.

claim: Libet and colleagues took the RP to be a marker for an unconscious decision to act.
source: Libet and colleagues took the RP to be a marker for an unconscious decision to act (Libet et al., 1983; Soon et al., 2008) that, once it begins, ballistically leads to action (Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006).
evidence: This is Libet's interpretation of the RP, supported by citations.

claim: Under Libet's interpretation, once the RP begins, it ballistically leads to action.
source: Libet and colleagues took the RP to be a marker for an unconscious decision to act (Libet et al., 1983; Soon et al., 2008) that, once it begins, ballistically leads to action (Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006).
evidence: This is part of Libet's interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: Under Libet's interpretation, the fact that RP onset precedes the report of conscious decision was taken as evidence that decisions about actions are made unconsciously.
source: Under that interpretation, the fact that RP onset precedes the report of the onset of the conscious decision to act was taken as evidence that decisions about actions are made unconsciously.
evidence: This describes the logical inference made by Libet from his findings.

claim: Libet's finding has been at the center of the free-will debate in neuroscience for almost four decades.
source: This finding has been at the center of the free-will debate in neuroscience for almost four decades, captivating scholars from many disciplines in and outside of academia (Frith et al., 2000; Frith and Haggard, 2018; Haggard, 2008; Jeannerod, 2006; Lau et al., 2004; Mele, 2006; Wegner, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by the extensive citations and the historical context provided.

claim: In previous RP studies, subjects were told to arbitrarily move their right hand or flex their right wrist, or to arbitrarily move either the right or left hand.
source: Critically, in the above studies, subjects were told to arbitrarily move their right hand or flex their right wrist; or they were instructed to arbitrarily move either the right or left hand (Haggard, 2008; Hallett, 2016; Roskies, 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental paradigms used in prior RP studies, supported by citations.

claim: In previous RP studies, subjects' decisions when and which hand to move were always unreasoned, purposeless, and bereft of any real consequence.
source: Thus, their decisions when and which hand to move were always unreasoned, purposeless, and bereft of any real consequence.
evidence: This characterizes the nature of decisions in prior RP studies.

claim: Many real-life decisions are deliberate—that is, reasoned, purposeful, and bearing consequences.
source: This stands in sharp contrast to many real-life decisions that are deliberate—that is, reasoned, purposeful, and bearing consequences (Ullmann-Margalit and Morgenbesser, 1977): which clothes to wear, what route to take to work, as well as more formative decisions about life partners, career choices, and so on.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and common knowledge about decision-making.

claim: Deliberate decisions have been widely studied in the field of neuroeconomics.
source: Deliberate decisions have been widely studied in the field of neuroeconomics (Kable and Glimcher, 2009; Sanfey et al., 2006) and in perceptual tasks (Gold and Shadlen, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroeconomics literature.

claim: Little has been done in neuroeconomics to assess the relation between decision-related activity, subjects' conscious experience of deciding, and the neural activity instantaneously contributing to this experience.
source: Yet, interestingly, little has been done in that field to assess the relation between decision-related activity, subjects' conscious experience of deciding, and the neural activity instantaneously contributing to this experience.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the neuroeconomics literature.

claim: Some studies compared internally driven and externally cued decisions, but these were typically arbitrary decisions and actions with no real implications.
source: Though some studies compared, for example, internally driven and externally cued decisions (Thut et al., 2000; Wisniewski et al., 2016), or stimulus-based and intention-based actions (Waszak et al., 2005), these were typically arbitrary decisions and actions with no real implications.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Direct comparisons between arbitrary and deliberate decisions are critical for the free will debate because it is deliberate, rather than arbitrary, decisions that are at the center of philosophical arguments about free will and moral responsibility.
source: Such direct comparisons are critical for the free will debate, because it is deliberate, rather than arbitrary, decisions that are at the center of philosophical arguments about free will and moral responsibility (Breitmeyer, 1985; Maoz and Yaffe, 2016; Roskies, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to philosophical literature.

claim: Deliberate decisions typically involve more conscious and lengthy deliberation and might thus be more tightly bound to conscious processes than arbitrary ones.
source: Deliberate decisions typically involve more conscious and lengthy deliberation and might thus be more tightly bound to conscious processes than arbitrary ones.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of deliberate decisions.

claim: If the RP is a marker for unconscious decisions, while deliberate decisions are driven more by conscious than by unconscious processes, then the RP might be substantially diminished, or even absent, for deliberate decisions.
source: Consequently, if the RP is a marker for unconscious decisions, while deliberate decisions are driven more by conscious than by unconscious processes, then the RP might be substantially diminished, or even absent, for deliberate decisions.
evidence: This is a logical prediction based on the hypothesis.

claim: A recent computational model claims that the RP reflects an artifact that results from a combination of biased sampling stemming from the methodology of calculating this component and autocorrelation in the EEG signal.
source: This model claims that the RP—which has been deemed a preparatory signal with a causal link to the upcoming movement—actually reflects an artifact that results from a combination of (i) biased sampling stemming from the methodology of calculating this component and (ii) autocorrelation (or smoothness) in the EEG signal.
evidence: This describes Schurger et al.'s model, which is cited.

claim: The RP is calculated by aligning EEG activity to movement onset, then segmenting a certain time duration around each movement onset, and finally averaging across all movements.
source: The RP is calculated by aligning EEG activity (typically in electrode Cz) to movement onset, then segmenting a certain time duration around each movement onset (i.e., epoching), and finally averaging across all movements.
evidence: This describes the standard methodology for calculating the RP.

claim: Schurger and colleagues demonstrated that RPs can be modeled using a mechanistic, stochastic, autocorrelated, drift-diffusion process that integrates noise to a bound.
source: Schurger and colleagues demonstrated that RPs can be modeled using a mechanistic, stochastic, autocorrelated, drift-diffusion process that integrates noise to a bound (or threshold; see Model section in Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schurger et al.'s work.

claim: In Schurger's model, it is only the threshold crossing that reflects decision completion and directly leads to action.
source: In the model, it is only the threshold crossing that reflects decision completion and directly leads to action.
evidence: This describes a key feature of Schurger's model.

claim: Within the framework of Schurger's model, the artificial accumulation of stochastic fluctuations toward a threshold is expected to occur for arbitrary decisions, but not for deliberate ones.
source: Importantly for our purposes, within the framework of the model, this artificial accumulation of stochastic fluctuations toward a threshold is expected to occur for arbitrary decisions, but not for deliberate ones.
evidence: This is a prediction derived from applying Schurger's model to the current study's paradigm.

claim: Unlike arbitrary decisions, deliberate decisions are generally not driven by random fluctuations but by the values of the decision alternatives.
source: Unlike arbitrary decisions, deliberate decisions are generally not driven by random fluctuations. Rather, it is the values of the decision alternatives that mainly drive the decision and ultimately lead to action.
evidence: This is a theoretical distinction between decision types.

claim: If the RP indeed reflects the artificial accumulation of stochastic fluctuations, a key prediction of the model is that no RP will be found for deliberate decisions.
source: Therefore, if the RP indeed reflects the artificial accumulation of stochastic fluctuations, as the model suggests, a key prediction of the model is that no RP will be found for deliberate decisions (see more below).
evidence: This is a prediction derived from the model.

claim: Demonstrating the absence of an RP in deliberate decisions challenges the interpretation of the RP as a general index of internal, unconscious decision-making.
source: Thus, demonstrating the absence of an RP in deliberate decisions challenges the interpretation of the RP as a general index of internal, unconscious decision-making; if this interpretation were correct, such a marker should have been found for all decision types.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: The absence of an RP in deliberate decisions questions the generalizability of any studies focused on arbitrary decisions to everyday, ecological, deliberate decisions.
source: What is more, and importantly, it questions the generalizability of any studies focused on arbitrary decisions to everyday, ecological, deliberate decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the implications of the findings.

claim: The absence of an RP in deliberate decisions challenges RP-based claims relating to moral responsibility, as moral responsibility can be ascribed only to deliberate decisions.
source: In particular, it challenges RP-based claims relating to moral responsibility (Haggard, 2008; Libet, 1985; Roskies, 2010), as moral responsibility can be ascribed only to deliberate decisions.
evidence: This is supported by citations and philosophical reasoning.

claim: The experiment utilized a donation-preference paradigm in which a pair of non-profit organizations were presented in each trial.
source: Our experiment utilized a donation-preference paradigm, in which a pair of non-profit organizations (NPOs) were presented in each trial.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In deliberate-decision trials, subjects chose to which NPO they would like to donate $1000.
source: In deliberate-decision trials, subjects chose to which NPO they would like to donate $1000.
evidence: This describes the deliberate condition in the experiment.

claim: In arbitrary-decision trials, both NPOs received an equal donation of $500, irrespective of subjects' key presses.
source: In arbitrary-decision trials, both NPOs received an equal donation of $500, irrespective of subjects' key presses (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the arbitrary condition in the experiment.

claim: In both conditions, subjects were instructed to report their decisions as soon as they made them.
source: In both conditions, subjects were instructed to report their decisions as soon as they made them, and their hands were placed on the response keys, to make sure they could do so as quickly as possible.
evidence: This describes the experimental instructions.

claim: The visual inputs and motor outputs were identical between deliberate and arbitrary decisions.
source: Notably, while the visual inputs and motor outputs were identical between deliberate and arbitrary decisions, the decisions' meaning for the subjects was radically different
evidence: This describes a key feature of the experimental design.

claim: Subjects' reaction times were substantially slower for deliberate than for arbitrary decisions.
source: As expected, subjects were substantially slower for deliberate (M = 2.33, SD = 0.51) than for arbitrary (M = 0.99, SD = 0.32) decisions (Figure 2, left; F(1,17)=114.87, p<0.0001 for the main effect of decision type).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A main effect of decision difficulty was found, with difficult decisions being slower than easy ones.
source: A main effect of decision difficulty was also found (F(1,17)=21.54, p<0.0005), with difficult decisions (M = 1.77, SD = 0.40) being slower than easy ones (M = 1.56, SD = 0.28).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Subjects were significantly slower for hard vs. easy decisions in the deliberate case but not for the arbitrary case.
source: Importantly, subjects were significantly slower for hard (M = 2.52, SD = 0.62) vs. easy (M = 2.13, SD = 0.44) decisions in the deliberate case (t(17)=4.78, p=0.0002), yet not for the arbitrary case (M = 1.00, SD = 0.34; M = 0.98, SD = 0.32, for hard and easy arbitrary decisions, respectively; t(17)=1.01, p=0.33; F(1,17)=20.85, p<0.0005 for the interaction between decision type and decision difficulty).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The roughly equal RTs between easy and hard arbitrary decisions provide evidence inconsistent with concerns that subjects were deliberating during arbitrary decisions.
source: What is more, the roughly equal RTs between easy and hard arbitrary decisions provide evidence inconsistent with concerns that subjects were deliberating during arbitrary decisions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Subjects were highly consistent with their own previous ratings when making deliberate decisions but not when making arbitrary ones.
source: As expected, subjects were highly consistent with their own, previous ratings when making deliberate decisions (M = 0.91, SD = 0.04), but not when making arbitrary ones (M = 0.52, SD = 0.04; Figure 2, right; F(1,17)=946.55, p<0.0001, BF = 2.32*1029) for the main effect of decision type.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A clear RP was found in arbitrary decisions in electrode Cz.
source: Focusing on the last 500 ms before movement onset for our statistical tests, we found a clear RP in arbitrary decisions, yet RP amplitude was not significantly different from 0 in deliberate decisions (Figure 3A; F(1,17)=11.86, p=0.003, BF = 309.21 for the main effect of decision type; in t-tests against 0 for this averaged activity in the different conditions, corrected for multiple comparisons, an effect was only found for arbitrary decisions (hard: t(17)=5.09, p=0.0001, BF = 307.38; easy: t(17)=5.75, p<0.0001, BF = 1015.84) and not for deliberate ones).
evidence: This is a primary EEG finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: RP amplitude was not significantly different from 0 in deliberate decisions.
source: Focusing on the last 500 ms before movement onset for our statistical tests, we found a clear RP in arbitrary decisions, yet RP amplitude was not significantly different from 0 in deliberate decisions (Figure 3A; F(1,17)=11.86, p=0.003, BF = 309.21 for the main effect of decision type; in t-tests against 0 for this averaged activity in the different conditions, corrected for multiple comparisons, an effect was only found for arbitrary decisions (hard: t(17)=5.09, p=0.0001, BF = 307.38; easy: t(17)=5.75, p<0.0001, BF = 1015.84) and not for deliberate ones).
evidence: This is a primary EEG finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A cluster-based nonparametric permutation analysis found a prolonged cluster of activation that reliably differed from 0 in both arbitrary conditions.
source: Using the default parameters (see Materials and methods), we found a prolonged cluster (~1.2 s) of activation that reliably differed from 0 in both arbitrary conditions (designated by horizontal blue-shaded lines above the x axis in Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an EEG finding from the experiment using cluster-based analysis.

claim: The cluster-based analysis revealed no clusters of activity differing from zero in either of the deliberate conditions.
source: The same analysis revealed no clusters of activity differing from zero in either of the deliberate conditions.
evidence: This is an EEG finding from the experiment using cluster-based analysis.

claim: Regressing voltage against time for the last 1000 ms before response onset, the downward trend was significant for arbitrary decisions but not for deliberate decisions.
source: In a similar manner, regressing voltage against time for the last 1000 ms before response onset, the downward trend was significant for arbitrary decisions (Figure 3B; p<0.0001, BF >1025 for both easy and hard conditions) but not for deliberate decisions, with the Bayes factor indicating conclusive evidence for no effect (hard: p>0.5, BF = 0.09; easy: p=0.35, BF = 0.31; all Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is an EEG finding from the experiment using regression analysis.

claim: 14 of the 18 subjects had significant downward slopes for arbitrary decisions when regressing voltage against time for every trial over the last 1000 ms before response onset.
source: Notably, this pattern of results was also manifested for single-subject analysis (Figure 4; 14 of the 18 subjects had significant downward slopes for arbitrary decisions—that is, p<0.05, Bonferroni corrected for multiple comparisons—when regressing voltage against time for every trial over the last 1000 ms before response onset
evidence: This is an EEG finding from single-subject analysis.

claim: Only 5 of the 18 subjects had significant downward slopes for the same regression analysis for deliberate decisions.
source: but only 5 of the 18 subjects had significant downward slopes for the same regression analysis for deliberate decisions
evidence: This is an EEG finding from single-subject analysis.

claim: The average slopes for deliberate and arbitrary decisions were −0.28 ± 0.25 and −1.9 ± 0.32, respectively, a significant difference.
source: In addition, the average slopes for deliberate and arbitrary decisions were −0.28 ± 0.25 and −1.9 ± 0.32 (mean ± SE), respectively, a significant difference: t(17)=4.55, p<0.001, BF = 380.02).
evidence: This is an EEG finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: A median split analysis using only the faster subjects in the deliberate condition and the slower subjects in the arbitrary condition showed a similar pattern of results to those over the whole dataset.
source: We then ran the same analysis using only the faster subjects in the deliberate condition (M = 1.91 s, SD = 0.25) and the slower subjects in the arbitrary condition (M = 1.25 s, SD = 0.23). If RT length affects RP amplitudes, we would expect the RP amplitudes to be more similar between these two groups. However, though there were only half the data points, a similar pattern of results to those over the whole dataset was observed (Figure 5A; compare to Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that RT differences do not drive the effect.

claim: No correlation was found between the difference between RPs in deliberate and arbitrary decisions and the difference between the RTs in these two conditions for each subject.
source: Again, if RT length affects RP amplitudes, we would expect differences between RTs in deliberate and arbitrary conditions to correlate with differences between RPs in the two conditions. But no correlation was found between the two measures (r = 0.28, t(16)=0.86, p=0.4).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that RT differences do not drive the effect.

claim: No significant differences were found in the number of saccades during deliberate and arbitrary trials.
source: Focusing again on the last 500 ms before response onset, we computed mean (± s.e.m.) SC values of 1.65 ± 0.07 and 1.67 ± 0.06 saccades for easy and hard deliberate decisions, respectively, and 1.69 ± 0.07 and 1.73 ± 0.07 saccades for easy and hard arbitrary decisions, respectively. We found no reliable differences between the number of saccades during deliberate and arbitrary trials (F(1,17)=2.56, p=0.13 for main effect of decision type).
evidence: This is a control analysis showing that eye movements do not drive the effect.

claim: In the LRP, no difference was found between the two decision types.
source: In this purely motor component, no difference was found between the two decision types and conclusive evidence against an effect of decision type was further found (Figure 7; all Fs < 0.35; BF = 0.299).
evidence: This is an EEG finding from the experiment, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The model's fit to the empirical RTs and consistencies were good.
source: The models' fit to the empirical RTs and consistencies were good (RT and consistency errors for deliberate easy and hard were 0.054 and 0.004 and 0.166 and 0.013 respectively; for arbitrary easy and hard they were 0.053 and 0.002, and 0.055 and 0.003, respectively; Figure 9A)
evidence: This is a modeling result showing the model fits the data well.

claim: The model predicted an RP-like activity for arbitrary decisions, but only a very slight slope for deliberate decisions.
source: The result was an RP-like activity for arbitrary decisions, but only a very slight slope for deliberate decisions (Figure 9B; both activities were flipped vertically, as in Schurger's model). This was in line with our empirical results (compare Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a modeling result that matches the empirical findings.

claim: The results suggest that two different neural mechanisms may be involved in arbitrary and deliberate decisions.
source: Our findings and the model thus suggest that two different neural mechanisms may be involved in arbitrary and deliberate decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: Deliberate, reasoned decision-making elicited activity in the prefrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Earlier literature demonstrated that deliberate, reasoned decision-making—which was mostly studied in the field of neuroeconomics (Kable and Glimcher, 2009) or using perceptual decisions (Gold and Shadlen, 2007)—elicited activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC; mainly the dorsolateral (DLPFC) part (Sanfey et al., 2003; Wallis and Miller, 2003) and ventromedial (VMPFC) part/orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) (Ramnani and Owen, 2004; Wallis, 2007) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) (Bush et al., 2000; Carter et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Arbitrary, meaningless decisions showed activations in the Supplementary Motor Area (SMA), alongside other frontal areas.
source: Arbitrary, meaningless decisions, in contrast, were mainly probed using variants of the Libet paradigm, showing activations in the Supplementary Motor Area (SMA), alongside other frontal areas like the medial frontal cortex (Brass and Haggard, 2008; Krieghoff et al., 2011) or the frontopolar cortex, as well as the posterior cingulate cortex (Fried et al., 2011; Soon et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results support the claim that the previous findings regarding the RP should be confined to arbitrary decisions and do not generalize to deliberate ones.
source: Therefore, at the very least, our results support the claim that the previous findings regarding the RP should be confined to arbitrary decisions and do not generalize to deliberate ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The results put the onus on attempts to generalize markers of upcoming action from arbitrary to deliberate decisions to demonstrate that those markers do indeed generalize.
source: Hence, such differences clearly challenge the generalizability of previous studies focusing on arbitrary decisions to deliberate ones, regardless of whether they were based on the RP or not. In other words, our results put the onus on attempts to generalize markers of upcoming action from arbitrary to deliberate decisions; it is on them now to demonstrate that those markers do indeed generalize.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The results challenge RP-based claims against free will in arbitrary decisions and the generalization of these claims to deliberate decisions.
source: Hence, our results challenge RP-based claims of Libet and follow-up literature against free will in arbitrary decisions and much more so the generalization of these claims to deliberate decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The study does not provide positive evidence that consciousness is more involved in deliberate decisions than in arbitrary ones.
source: It should be noted that our study does not provide positive evidence that consciousness is more involved in deliberate decisions than in arbitrary ones; such a strong claim requires further evidence, perhaps from future research.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The RP does not capture all unconscious processes that precede conscious awareness.
source: To be clear, and following the above, we do not claim that the RP captures all unconscious processes that precede conscious awareness.
evidence: This is a clarification of the scope of the claims.

claim: The results provide evidence against the claim that the RP represents unconscious motor-preparatory activity before any kind of decision.
source: However, some have suggested that the RP represents unconscious motor-preparatory activity before any kind of decision (e.g., Libet, 1985). But our results provide evidence against that claim, as we do not find an RP before deliberate decisions, which also entail motor preparation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In deliberate decisions, it is likely that there are neural precursors of upcoming actions which are unrelated to the RP.
source: Furthermore, in deliberate decisions in particular, it is likely that there are neural precursors of upcoming actions—possibly involving the above neural circuits as well as circuits that represents values—which are unrelated to the RP (the lack of such precursors is not merely implausible; it implies dualism: Mudrik and Maoz, 2015; Wood, 1985).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations.

claim: The study did not attempt to clock subjects' conscious decision to move.
source: Note also that we did not attempt to clock subjects' conscious decision to move. Rather, we instructed them to hold their hands above the relevant keyboard keys and press their selected key as soon as they made up their mind.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the experiment.

claim: Clock monitoring was demonstrated to have an effect on RP size.
source: But, even more importantly, clock monitoring was demonstrated to have an effect on RP size (Miller et al., 2011), so it could potentially confound our results (Maoz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The longer RTs in deliberate decisions suggest that more complex mental processes took place before deliberate and not arbitrary decisions.
source: But this interpretation is unlikely because the longer RTs in deliberate decisions suggest, if anything, that more complex mental processes (conscious or unconscious) took place before deliberate and not arbitrary decisions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: If the RP is not present before deliberate action, it does not seem to be a necessary link in the general causal chain leading to action.
source: If the RP is not present before deliberate action, it does not seem to be a necessary link in the general causal chain leading to action.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: The results and model are in line with the interpretation that the RP represents the accumulation of noisy, random fluctuations that drive arbitrary decisions, whereas deliberate decisions are mainly driven by the values associated with the decision alternatives.
source: Our results and our model are in line with that interpretation and expand it to decisions that include both when and which hand to move. They suggest that the RP represents the accumulation of noisy, random fluctuations that drive arbitrary decisions, whereas deliberate decisions are mainly driven by the values associated with the decision alternatives (Maoz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental and modeling results.

claim: The drift-diffusion model was based on the assumption that every decision can be driven by a component reflecting the values of the decision alternatives or by another component representing noise.
source: Our drift-diffusion model was based on the assumption that every decision can be driven by a component reflecting the values of the decision alternatives (i.e., subjects' support for the two NPOs we presented) or by another component representing noise—random fluctuations in neural activity.
evidence: This describes the assumptions underlying the model.

claim: In arbitrary decisions, action selection and timing depend on when the accumulation of noise crosses the decision threshold for the congruent and incongruent decision alternatives.
source: The value component plays little to no role in arbitrary decisions, so action selection and timing depend on when the accumulation of noise crosses the decision threshold for the congruent and incongruent decision alternatives.
evidence: This describes how the model accounts for arbitrary decisions.

claim: In deliberate decisions, the value component drives the decisions, while the noise component plays little to no role.
source: In deliberate decisions, in contrast, the value component drives the decisions, while the noise component plays little to no role.
evidence: This describes how the model accounts for deliberate decisions.

claim: The model challenges RP-based claims against free will in both arbitrary and deliberate decisions.
source: Our model therefore challenges RP-based claims against free will in both arbitrary and deliberate decisions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: Twenty healthy subjects participated in the study.
source: Twenty healthy subjects participated in the study.
evidence: This describes the sample size.

claim: The data from 18 subjects was analyzed; two subjects were excluded from the analysis.
source: The data from 18 subjects was analyzed; two subjects were excluded from our analysis (see Sample size and exclusion criteria below).
evidence: This describes the final sample size after exclusions.

claim: The experiment was approved by Caltech's Institutional Review Board (14–0432; Neural markers of deliberate and random decisions).
source: The experiment was approved by Caltech's Institutional Review Board (14–0432; Neural markers of deliberate and random decisions), and informed consent was obtained from all participants after the experimental procedures were explained to them.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.

claim: The 2 × 2 design was decision type (arbitrary vs. deliberate) by decision difficulty (easy vs. hard).
source: Our 2 × 2 design was therefore decision type (arbitrary vs. deliberate) by decision difficulty (easy vs. hard).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.
